sections.title: Name and identification limits
sections.text: Russula xerampelina (Schaeff.) Fr. belongs to the Russulaceae. Recent phylogenetic work recognizes several species within subsection Xerampelinae; the name R. xerampelina has often been misapplied to similar North American russulas. This entry follows the Eurasian taxon concept supported by current studies. A photograph alone cannot confirm a russula: spores, microscopic characters and habitat information may be needed.

sections.title: Cap and form
sections.text: This is a stout brittlegill with a cap about 5–15 cm across, sometimes larger, convex at first and later expanded, often depressed at the centre. The smooth surface may be viscid in wet weather and matte as it dries. Wine-red, purple and reddish-brown are common, but pigmentation varies widely and may be brown, olive, yellowish or tan. Colour alone does not identify the species; some russulas formerly grouped under this name are now treated as separate species.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are attached to the stem, close to moderately crowded, brittle, cream at first and later pale yellow to ochre; they may brown when bruised and some fork near the stem. The stout stem is whitish to cream, often with a pink flush, and slowly browns where rubbed or handled. The firm, pale flesh may also turn rusty brown in air. A fishy, crab-like or shrimp-like odour is often stronger in mature or collected specimens, but may be absent in young ones; the taste is described as mild.

sections.title: Habitat and caution
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal russula grows on the ground in woodland, especially with conifers. Recent data associate the Eurasian taxon particularly with Scots pine, and also with spruce and fir; host records and fruiting periods depend on region. Subsection Xerampelinae contains several closely related species that are difficult to separate by cap colour alone. The DGfM and VAPKO lists classify the traditional broad concept of R. xerampelina (sensu lato) as edible; they do not certify the strict Eurasian taxon used here or identify any particular specimen. Do not eat a wild mushroom based on a photograph or this entry; ask an expert to confirm it.

traits: Stout russula with a cap about 5–15 cm across, sometimes larger, convex then expanded and depressed at the centre
Highly variable colour: commonly wine-red or purple, but also reddish-brown, olive, yellowish or tan; colour alone is not diagnostic
Attached, brittle gills, cream then pale yellow to ochre, sometimes forked near the stem and browning when bruised
Stout whitish stem, often pink-flushed, slowly browning when handled; firm pale flesh may brown in air
Often fishy or shellfish-like odour in mature or collected specimens, sometimes absent in young ones; taste described as mild
Ectomycorrhizal, especially associated with conifers in its Eurasian range, including Scots pine
safetyNote: The DGfM and VAPKO lists concern the traditional broad concept of Russula xerampelina (sensu lato); they do not certify the strict Eurasian species used here or the identification of any particular specimen. Closely related russulas are difficult to distinguish and cap colours vary widely. Do not eat a wild mushroom based on a photo or this entry; have an expert confirm the identification.
